analysis.one_liner: Blocks the EPA and Army Corps from finalizing or enforcing their Clean Water Act waters rule.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 262-152, but the Senate never took it up, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: In 2014 the EPA and the Army Corps of Engineers proposed a rule to define which streams, wetlands, and other waters count as 'waters of the United States' under the Clean Water Act, which would determine where federal pollution permits are required. This bill would prohibit the agencies from finalizing, using, or enforcing that rule or anything substantially like it, and would void any enforcement action based on it. It would also require the agencies to withdraw a separate rule giving agriculture a permitting exemption, and instead go through a months-long consultation with state and local officials before proposing a new definition, with any recommendation requiring unanimous consensus.
analysis.who_benefits: If enacted, the bill would spare farmers, real estate developers, homebuilders, and energy and mining companies from a wider set of federal permitting requirements and from potential Clean Water Act enforcement actions on small streams and wetlands. State and local officials would gain a larger formal role in defining federal water jurisdiction.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Farmers, developers, energy and mining companies

how_it_helps.text: The bill flatly prohibits the Army Corps and EPA from developing, finalizing, adopting, implementing, administering, or enforcing the proposed 'Waters of the United States' rule published April 21, 2014, and a related 2012 guidance document [S5].

It goes further than a simple delay: it bars the agencies from using the proposed rule, any successor, or 'any substantially similar proposed rule or guidance' as the basis for any Clean Water Act rulemaking or enforcement decision, and makes any such decision grounds for being vacated in court [S5].

It requires the agencies to withdraw the April 2014 interpretive rule on agricultural conservation practice exemptions and to apply the Clean Water Act without it, ending the agencies' clarification of what farming activities need no permit [S5].

In place of the rule, the agencies would have to consult state and local officials and could publish a recommendation on the scope of covered waters only if consensus were reached among the agencies and the consulted officials; failure to reach consensus would itself become the report [S5].

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on people downstream of unprotected streams and wetlands, including the roughly one in three Americans whose drinking water draws on the seasonal and headwater streams the proposed rule aimed to cover, who would lose a clarified federal backstop against upstream pollution. It would also shift the burden of ambiguity back to landowners, citizen groups, and state agencies trying to figure out case by case which waters are protected.

drawbacks.text: By voiding any 'substantially similar' rule and any enforcement action relying on it, the bill would not merely postpone the rule but lock in the pre-2014 ambiguity, leaving decades-old questions about which tributaries, seasonal streams, and nearby wetlands are protected under the Clean Water Act unresolved [S5].

The consensus requirement is a structural obstacle: the agencies could publish a recommendation only if agreement were reached among the EPA, the Army Corps, and state and local officials, and any failure to agree simply gets documented rather than resolved, making a new rulemaking hard to ever complete [S5].

Supporters of the underlying rule argued that the streams and wetlands in question feed drinking water supplies for roughly one in three Americans, so a statutory bar on clarifying their protection is a cost to the public, not a paperwork saving. This is the claim the bill's opponents made on the House floor and in the motion to recommit, which would have added a section protecting the quality of water for public water supplies and agricultural uses and mitigating drought; it failed 177-235 [S8, S7].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers real, concentrated relief to farming, real estate, and extractive interests by taking a broad swath of waters off the table for federal permitting and permanently barring this rule and any close copy of it. Against that, it leaves in place the very legal uncertainty everyone agrees exists, replaces the rule with a consensus process that is almost designed to deadlock, and removes a clarified federal protection for the upstream waters that feed drinking supplies. There is a fair argument that the proposed rule reached too far and needed rework, but this bill does not rework it; it prohibits it and its descendants.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 262-152 on September 9, 2014, but the Senate only read and calendared it and never voted, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced July 11, 2014 by Rep. Steve Southerland (R-FL) with 120 cosponsors (115 Republicans, 5 Democrats), and was reported by the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee by voice vote on July 31 [S7, S6, S3].
On September 9, 2014, the House passed it on a recorded vote of 262-152, with 227 of 232 voting Republicans in favor and only 35 of 199 voting Democrats in favor [S9].
A Democratic motion to recommit the bill with instructions to add water-quality protections for public water supplies failed 177-235, with 177 Democrats in favor and no Republicans [S8].

The Senate received the bill on September 10, read it twice, and placed it on the Senate calendar under General Orders on September 11, where it stayed until the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 without a vote [S7, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill never became law, so the industries that would have gained from it — agriculture, real estate development, and energy and mining — got nothing from this bill, while people who drink water from the streams the rule would cover kept the existing federal protections. The underlying rule later moved forward on its own track, so the practical status quo of contested jurisdiction persisted.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage split almost entirely by party: 227 of 232 voting Republicans voted yes against only 35 of 199 voting Democrats, and the Democratic motion to recommit drew zero Republican votes [S9, S8].

industries.note: Farmers would be spared the possibility of federal permitting for ditches, ponds, and drainage features near covered waters, and the bill withdraws the 2014 interpretive rule that clarified farm conservation exemptions. The gain is freedom from permit requirements that the agencies argued were needed to keep upstream pollution out of drinking-water sources downstream.

Developers faced Section 404 permit costs and delay on sites containing small streams and wetlands; the bill bars the rule that would expand those requirements and voids enforcement based on it or any similar rule, at the cost of leaving downstream communities with less protection.

Oil and gas, coal, and mining operations would avoid expanded federal permitting and Clean Water Act enforcement on smaller waters, saving compliance costs that critics said come out of water quality for the public.

industries.industry: Municipal water utilities and downstream water systems
industries.note: Utilities and the communities they serve would lose the clarified federal protection for headwater and seasonal streams that feed drinking supplies, keeping pollution control of those waters ambiguous and contested case by case.

industries.industry: Environmental protection agencies (EPA and Army Corps)
industries.note: The bill strips both agencies of authority to finalize, enforce, or even base future decisions on the rule, and imposes a consensus process that requires agreement from consulted state and local officials before any recommendation can be published, which critics viewed as a veto over federal water policy.
